tldr: We propose a framework that requires zero human demonstrations, zero policy pre-training, and zero known 3D models. By leveraging a 3D mesh generated from a single-view image alongside a contact action space, it runs reinforcement learning in simulation for just minutes (averaging 119 seconds) and achieves an 87% success rate on real-world manipulation.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of ZeroBot. An image-to-3D model reconstructs a complete mesh in seconds from a single-view image taken by a wrist camera. Large-scale parallel reinforcement learning runs in a simulator, and the learned contact action space and policy transfer zero-shot directly to the real robot.
overview:
When solving tasks that move an unknown object to a goal pose, traditional reinforcement learning takes enormous amounts of time for real-world data collection and safety supervision. In simulation learning (Sim2Real), preparing high-precision 3D assets and manual scanning have been major bottlenecks.

The authors tackled this by integrating web-scale visual pre-trained models (image-to-3D generative models) into the bridge from the real world to simulation (Real2Sim). From a single RGB-D image, a complete 3D mesh including the unseen back side is generated in about 10 seconds, real scale is recovered using depth information, and the asset is placed in the simulator. Furthermore, to dramatically speed up training, they developed a "contact action space" that samples contact states along surface normals of the generated mesh and uses the reinforcement learning value function to warp directly to promising contact locations to start exploration.

Evaluation was conducted using a real Franka Research 3 arm across 6 tasks, including multi-stage manipulation where a book is shifted and then grasped, rolling a can up a ramp, and grasping a tumbler whose handle is partially occluded. Starting from a "zero scratch" state with no human demonstrations and no policy pre-training, ZeroBot achieved an 87% real-world success rate with an average training time of 119 seconds. This demonstrates that a generative mesh from a single view is vastly superior for Sim2Real transfer compared to retrieval-based or partial point cloud meshes.
contributions: Formulated the problem setting and proposed the ZeroBot framework to learn real-world manipulation in minutes using only a single-view image and a goal pose, without human demonstrations, pre-trained policies, or known 3D models.
Constructed a digital twin of the real environment in seconds by combining InstantMesh for single-view mesh generation with Foundation Pose for pose tracking, enabling zero-shot Sim2Real transfer.

Developed a Contact Action Space that leverages generated mesh geometry and the learned value function to bypass fruitless free-space exploration and immediately initiate interaction from high-value contact states.

Demonstrated through real-world experiments covering grasping, pushing, rolling, articulated objects, and multi-stage manipulation that generated meshes yield a higher success rate (87%) than mesh retrieval or partial point clouds.

sections.heading: RL Exploration Efficiency and the Evolution of Real2Sim
sections.summary: To address the slow data collection of real-world reinforcement learning, Sim2Real and Real2Sim leveraging parallel simulator computing are drawing attention. While conventional Real2Sim relies on manual scans or model retrieval, this work incorporates 3D generative priors derived from 2D diffusion models to autonomously generate simulation environments instantaneously from a single view.
sections.details:
Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) has always faced challenges with data collection efficiency, safety, and automated resets. Efficient action spaces using spatial grounding and discretization have been investigated to solve these, but training generalized models usually requires days. Simulation, on the other hand, allows running large numbers of agents in parallel according to available compute to accelerate learning.

In Real2Sim research that reconstructs real scenes inside simulators, visual reconstruction using NeRF or 3D Gaussian Splatting and physical parameter identification for friction, mass, and joints have been proposed. However, most conventional methods require humans to manually scan around the object or pre-position multiple cameras, and they cannot complete occluded surfaces.

Image-to-3D generative models based on 2D image diffusion models, which have recently made breakthroughs, use powerful web-scale visual priors to predict a complete 3D mesh—including the unseen backside—from a single-view partial observation. While this generative technology has primarily been used for offline scene generation or reconstructing human demonstration videos, ZeroBot integrates it into a real-time online training pipeline, enabling instant robot learning from scratch.

sections.heading: From 3D Mesh Generation to Parallel Reinforcement Learning via Contact Action Space
sections.summary: ZeroBot consists of three phases. First, it generates a mesh from single-view RGB-D and aligns it to real scale. Next, it performs large-scale parallel RL in minutes using a contact action space driven by the generated mesh. Finally, it transfers value-guided contact planning and policy execution zero-shot to the real robot.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Setting and Assumptions
The robot is provided only with a single RGB-D image $\mathcal{I}$ of the target object and a relative goal pose from the object's initial pose $\mathcal{T}_{OG} \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$. No human demonstration data, pre-trained policies, or prior CAD models are used. The background (such as a shelf) is assumed to be scanned automatically and fixed by the wrist camera before placing the object, starting from a viewpoint where the target object is clearly visible.

### III-B Simulation Construction with Generative Priors
The target object in the camera image is segmented with SAM 2, and InstantMesh generates a 3D mesh from the RGB image in just 10 seconds. Because InstantMesh alone cannot determine absolute scale, depth point clouds from the same viewpoint and the generated mesh are aligned using batched ICP (Iterative Closest Point) to accurately recover the mesh's geometric scale. Since end-to-end learning outputting actions directly from images does not converge within minutes, the design uses Foundation Pose with the generated mesh to track the object's 6D pose, training and executing a state-based policy.

### III-C Simulation Learning and Real Deployment via Contact Action Space
Isaac Gym serves as the simulator, training across 256 parallel environments using PPO. As a reward function, "Goal Flow" is consistently adopted to minimize the vector norm from each point on the object to its goal position, eliminating the need to tune weights between position and rotation.

The most critical design here is the "Contact Action Space." In standard end-effector control, the robot wastes much of its simulator time traveling through empty space before touching the object. Therefore, candidate contact poses based on surface normals are sampled directly from the generated mesh surface, and cuRobo filters them for collision-free valid states $s$. The training value function $V(s)$ evaluates these states, and the robot transitions directly to a high-value contact state before the policy actions begin.

During training, exploration is driven by a probability $p(s)$ combining temperature-scaled Softmax and warmup, and the policy learns residual actions added to the Goal Flow vectors toward the target after contact. During real-world deployment, the value function $V(s)$—which is typically discarded—is reused directly to determine the optimal initial contact pose. After a safe approach planned by cuRobo, the trained policy is executed.

(1) Generates a 3D model with InstantMesh from single-view RGB-D and rescales it using depth, (2) runs parallel RL on Isaac Gym using Goal Flow reward and contact action space, (3) selects contact poses with the learned value function $V(s)$ and executes zero-shot on the real robot.

After approaching the highest-value contact pose (3–4), the object is manipulated with residual action policy $\pi(s)$ (5).

sections.heading: Validation Across 6 Real Tasks and Fast Learning Ablations
sections.summary: Using a Franka Research 3 arm, 6 real-world tasks involving complex grasping, pushing, and rolling were evaluated. ZeroBot achieved an average training time of 119 seconds and an 87% real success rate, significantly outperforming mesh retrieval and partial point cloud approaches. The contact action space was confirmed as the decisive factor for accelerated learning.
sections.details:
### IV-A Research Questions and Experimental Setup
The evaluation utilized a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm with a wrist-mounted camera (RealSense D435) and an external tracking camera (D455). Two NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs were used: one for policy training and one for pose tracking. The 6 tasks evaluated were:
- MultiStageBook: A two-stage task pushing a book off a box to create clearance, then lifting it
- PushUpRamp: Dynamic balancing task rolling a soda can up an incline
- SlideBowl: Sliding task pushing the unseen far side of a bowl to pull it closer
- NovelPoses: Grasping and lifting a tea bottle across a 20×20 cm placement variation
- PullFromShelf: Pulling a bottle from deep within a narrow shelf while avoiding collisions
- GraspHandle: Grasping a tumbler whose handle is facing away and only partially visible

For baselines, we compared against "ZB-NoPrior," which uses a partial mesh reconstructed via Poisson reconstruction from a single-view point cloud without 3D priors, and "ACDC-NN," which retrieves and substitutes the nearest-neighbor CAD model from images.

### IV-B Real-World Evaluation Results
ZeroBot achieved an overall success rate of 87%. ZB-NoPrior failed on PushUpRamp because the missing backside of the can prevented rolling, and it collided with real objects during grasping tasks. ACDC-NN failed to grasp items with specialized shapes like the tumbler due to mismatched handle geometry. ZeroBot accurately completed geometry that was not directly visible—such as the bowl's back side and the tumbler's self-occluded handle—demonstrating superior Sim2Real transfer.

### IV-C Learning Speed and Design Component Analysis
In ablations on the SlideBowl task, conventional Cartesian control (NoContAct) showed nearly a 0% success rate even after 30 minutes. Adding contact-promoting auxiliary rewards (NoContAct-Rew) or trajectory optimization (TrajOpt-Rew) either learned slowly or plateaued early. Compared to CRL-Octree, which zooms in using an octree search, ZeroBot's contact action space ramped up vastly faster, reaching a 100% simulation success rate in just minutes.

### IV-D Extension to Articulated Objects
For opening a microwave door, ZeroBot was compared with an Oracle mesh created by manually scanning 164 multi-view images (using Polycam, mesh generation took 443 seconds). ZeroBot's single-view generated mesh (mesh generation took 23 seconds) achieved an 80% success rate, approaching the Oracle's 100% success rate while demonstrating the practicality of autonomous operation in dramatically less time.

sections.heading: Current Limitations and Future Horizons
sections.summary: Primary limitations include the geometric fidelity of current image-to-3D models, static background assumptions, and treating object mass and joint parameters as known. Future directions include incorporating multi-view inputs and integrating automated estimation for physical properties and articulated structures.
sections.details:
While ZeroBot demonstrated very strong results, several assumptions and limitations remain:

- Geometric Precision Limits: Although state-of-the-art image-to-3D models are used, millimeter-level accuracy is not yet achieved, leaving challenges for tasks requiring extremely precise mating. Upgrading to multi-view inputs or occlusion-aware generative models would be effective remedies.
- Physical and Joint Parameter Assumptions: In this work, object mass is kept fixed, and microwave joint parameters (axis of rotation and limits) are treated as known. Combining physical parameter estimation and automated kinematic structure identification could enable full autonomy.
- Static Scene Assumptions: The system assumes a pre-scanned background via the wrist camera; extending this to dynamic, cluttered environments with multiple objects is an important future problem.

sections.heading: Summary: New Frontiers in Autonomous RL Opened by Generative Models
sections.summary: We proposed ZeroBot, which learns real-world robot manipulation in minutes with zero demos, zero pre-training, and zero CAD models. Combining image-to-3D generative models with a contact action space pushes autonomous robot skill acquisition significantly forward.
sections.details: This paper presented ZeroBot, a Real2Sim framework that instantly bootstraps simulation from a single-view image using image-to-3D generative models and acquires policies via reinforcement learning. By leveraging full 3D geometry to eliminate wasteful exploration, the "contact action space" enables an 87% real-world success rate with an average training time of just 119 seconds. Instead of relying on manual scanning or model retrieval, this milestone clearly proves the power of a "learn on the fly and act immediately" robotic system driven by the visual knowledge of foundation models.

takeaways: 3D generative priors from 2D image diffusion models complete unseen backsides and serve as powerful geometric engines for robot Real2Sim.
Sampling contact states from the object mesh surface and selecting promising candidates using the RL value function dramatically cuts exploration time.
The PPO value function used during training can be directly repurposed during real-world deployment as an evaluation function to select safe, efficient approach poses.
Ad-hoc 3D mesh generation from a single view yields higher Sim2Real success rates than partial point cloud meshes or retrieving pre-existing CAD models.
limitations: Object weight and friction coefficients are treated as uniform fixed values, with no automated physical parameter estimation included.
Kinematic axes and range-of-motion limits for articulated objects are assumed to be provided beforehand.
The background environment must be static and pre-scanned without the target object present.
